newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico reports unspectacular first quarter growth.
newsitem.headline: Mexico reports unspectacular first quarter growth.

text.p: Mexico on Monday reported first quarter economic growth of slightly more than 5 percent, indicating a continuing but unspectacular recovery from recession.

Mexico, snapping at Japan's heels to become the United States' second largest trading partner after Canada, plunged into crisis in 1995 after a bungled peso devaluation. Gross domestic product numbers only moved into the black in the second quarter last year.
First quarter GDP growth for 1997 emerged on Monday at 5.1 percent -- in line with downward revisions in analysts' forecasts after the government moved to deflate expectations last week.

"Today's figure was in line with the lower expectations of last week ... analysts had (previously) expected stronger growth but this is not a bad figure," said Enrique Ramirez, economist at Santander Investment in Mexico City.
"We can see that the base of economic growth is becoming broader and this is positive," he added.
But Denis Parisien, vice president for Latin American Research at Bankers Trust in New York, was more bearish.
"My impression is it's not terribly impressive," he said. "The spectacular numbers of the second half of 1996 are no more... .Now we have to adjust our expectations."
Seasonal adjustments -- to remove the distorting effect of last year's numbers that looked extra-robust against 1995's weak base year -- made the picture look even less rosy, he added.
"If you seasonally adjust 5.1 percent, the quarter-on-quarter growth is about flat (from the fourth quarter of 1996 to the first quarter of 1997)," Parisien said.
Monday's GDP number followed swiftly after Thursday's disappointing 6.2 percent result for first quarter industrial output.
But Monday's GDP number was on balance neutral for the market, analysts said. Some even saw reason for optimism in the 5 percent growth clocked up in the services sector.
Analysts at market consultants IDEA had forecast growth in services of around 3.8 percent.

The services component was itself boosted by a 5.6 percent year-on-year rise in the commerce, restaurant and hotel sector, a 7.3 percent rise in transport, storage and communications, and a still poor but bigger-than-expected increase in financial sector services of 4.7 percent.
Some analysts took this to indicate a broader participation in Mexico's gradual climb out of recession.
"Services are a reflection of the domestic market -- these figures show that the internal market is slowly recovering," Santander's Ramirez said.
